sentences.gloss_en: Welcome to a new explainer where we simplify the most complex topics.
Today we open the black box of AI and understand together exactly what happens inside it.
From computing a single neuron by hand all the way to the Transformer.
Trust me, there is no magic here; it is all just calculations and numbers.
Ready? Let's go; our agenda is very quick.
We start with neural network basics, then see how we prepare the text for the model.
Then we get inside the Transformer, then prediction and generation, and finally the core LLM concepts and prompting with its layers.
Part one: neural network basics, or the basic building blocks.
As agreed, there is no magic; it is all math and data.
So how do we compute a single neuron?
It is very simple: the equation is W times X plus B.
We take our inputs, for example the number of the customer's orders or their LTV.
We multiply them by the weights, then add the bias to them.
This sum then passes through something called an activation function, and all of this is computed step by step.
So that the neuron gives us its opinion on the result at the end.
Why do you think the activation function is necessary?
Without it, simply, the layers all collapse and become just a straight line.
Because a linear function followed by a linear function gives a linear result again.
It starts to bend and curves get formed (the opening words were lost in the audio).
And that is literally what lets it understand the patterns and complex data that no straight line could ever capture.
Let's count the numbers and parameters together to know where the size of this model comes from.
If we have 3 inputs going into 2 neurons, we get 6 weights plus 2 bias, so 8.
And when these 2 neurons go to the output neuron 1, we add 2 weights and 1 bias.
That is 3 more, so the total is exactly 11.
See how? By counting them we understand exactly how the network is built.
Great. Now how does the model learn?
This loop starts with a forward pass, from which we get a prediction.
And we measure how wrong we were, which is what we call the loss.
Here comes the role of backpropagation: we go in exactly the reverse direction and ask with the chain rule.
If we move this weight a little, how will the loss change?
Simply put, that is the gradient, just a slope with a sign.
It tells us to move the weight in whichever direction reduces this error.
The size of the step we take is the learning rate.
At first you will find the loss going down calmly and smoothly, but focus with me.
As soon as the learning rate passes 0.35, the curve scatters completely and blows up.
The calculations break and the model collapses.
By the way, this loop is the foundation of any model in the world, at large scale.
Part two: preparing the text for the model.
These networks do not understand words; they only understand numbers.
So we must convert any text into numbers first.
This point is extremely important.
The model does not see words or letters; it sees something called tokens.
These tokens are determined by frequency.
So one token is roughly 4 characters, or three quarters of an English word.
Then each token is turned into a vector, which is the embedding.
And we add its position in the sentence; without this position the model would not know the word order at all.
We move on to part three: about the Transformer, specifically the attention mechanism, which is the heart of the whole technology.
Suppose we designed a very small Transformer so that we can understand it.
Its d_model is 8, it has 2 heads, d_head is 4, and it has 1 block only.
In total, 696 weights.
The advantage here is that we can follow the data step by step through 14 detailed stages.
And we see the numbers being multiplied with each other right before our eyes.
Here the Attention process begins.
Each token produces 3 things: Query, Key and Value.
The idea is that the query of the token we are standing at starts scanning and asks the key of every other token in the sentence.
This process gives us a grid, or heat map, of width 8, full of raw scores telling us exactly who attends to whom.
But here there is a catch: a model that predicts the next word cannot look at the future, right?
That is why we put a causal mask, in a triangle shape, that switches off the upper half of this grid entirely.
Then comes the softmax function, which turns these scores into weights, and the result is very precise.
The sum of each row must come out to exactly one, 1.000, which sets the share of attention for each earlier word.
Now we reach the residual stream, the main pathway of information that every block reads from and writes to.
Multi-head attention makes each head focus on a specific relationship between the tokens.
Then they mix the values with the weights and write this result straight into the residual stream.
Part four: prediction and word generation; here we will see how the model works (one word is unclear in the audio).
And remember, it does not give us a definitive answer; it gives us a probability distribution.
So how do we control this distribution?
We have the temperature: if we set it from 0 to 0.3...
The distribution becomes sharp and specific, which is perfect for data analysis.
But if we raise it above 0.7, the distribution spreads out and there is more creativity and diversity.
There is also top-p, which trims the tail of this distribution so that the text stays logical.
We take one token by sampling and append it, and this whole circle goes round again from the start.
Part five: the core concepts of LLMs, or large language models.
When we scale up, these LLMs are nothing but the same Transformer we explained, only at a giant size and run on huge data.
There are some terms we need to know.
The context window, for example, is the maximum number of tokens the model can see at one time, and it ranges from 4000 to 128000.
And there is hallucination, which happens when the model says very convincing but completely wrong things.
That is why we need grounding, or to tie the outputs to real sources, like the RAG technique.
Part six and last with us: prompting and its practical applications.
How we put everything we understood into practice at work: writing the right prompt, not just chatting with the model.
We must give it a structured format (the word is unclear in the audio), like a daily summary, give it the schema, and assign it a role persona.
That means we ask it to talk to us as an engineer or as a manager.
We use techniques like zero-shot and few-shot.
And most important of all, we must always validate the results: extract the SQL or parse the JSON to make sure it is all sound.
Let's see a practical application: we have two tools, the InsightsGenerator.
It takes daily metrics such as 156 orders, revenue 45890 and AOV 294.
And it produces a summary in business language, with a very low temperature of 0.3 to be more precise.
The second tool is the AnomalyExplainer, which investigates the strange numbers.
The models here rely on external tools that fetch this data so that they do not hallucinate.
Imagine with me: the expected revenue on Sunday was 50,000, but the actual came out at only 28,500.
The model here went into the data.
And it explained to us that the cause was timeouts in the payment gateway from 2 to 4 in the afternoon, because of a snowstorm.
All of this explanation comes out based on the real data.
This sentence is the takeaway for anyone who works with data.
SQL does the calculations, and the LLM just explains.
The model is not an accurate calculator; the code is what computes correctly.
The role of the LLM is to phrase, summarize and clarify these numbers for us in a smooth way.
And with that we have reached the end of the explainer; we walked the journey from when we computed a neuron by hand.
We saw the learning rate problems, took the transformer apart step by step, and ended up at the prompt templates.
After all these numbers and details have become transparent and clear in front of you.
I wonder what you could build with these tools.
All the options are open for experimentation.
Thank you so much, and see you in a new explainer.
